name: Knight School
blurb: Openings, the six tricks that win pieces, and three checkmates you can always do.
who: For a player whose games are decided by leaving pieces where they can be taken.

lessons.name: Wake Up the Team
lessons.big: Take the middle, bring the pieces out, castle.

steps.text: Three jobs in the first few moves. Middle, pieces out, king safe.

steps.ask: Take the middle. Push a centre pawn two squares.
steps.hint: The e pawn or the d pawn, two squares forward.
steps.wrongSay: A centre pawn. The e file or the d file.

steps.text: Knights before bishops. A knight has fewer good squares, so it is easier to choose.

steps.cap: Six moves in: middle taken, four pieces out, king tucked away behind three pawns.

steps.ask: Should you bring the queen out on move two?

choices.text: No. Everybody chases her and you lose time
Yes, she is the strongest piece

steps.why: Every attack on her costs you a move, and they develop a piece while you run.

steps.ask: By roughly which move should your king have castled?

choices.text: About move ten
It can wait until the end

steps.why: A king in the middle is where all the lines meet. Get him out early.

steps.goal: Play a game. Take the middle, get your pieces out, and castle by move ten.

steps.text: Middle, pieces, king. Every game.

lessons.name: The Italian Game
lessons.big: Point your bishop at the weak spot.

steps.text: One opening, learned properly, is worth twenty half remembered.

steps.cap: The Italian Game. Watch the bishop on c4 and where it is pointing.

notes.5: 3. Bc4 — the bishop aims at f7, the weakest square they have.
notes.7: 4. c3 — making room to build a big centre with d4 later.
notes.11: 6. O-O — king safe, and now the rook can come to e1.
notes.13: 7. Re1 — every piece has a job. That is the whole opening.

steps.ask: Start it. Pawn to e4.
steps.hint: The king's pawn, two squares.
steps.wrongSay: e4. Two squares up the e file.

steps.ask: Now the knight. Nf3, attacking their pawn.
steps.hint: Knights before bishops.
steps.wrongSay: The knight on g1, out to f3.

steps.ask: Now the bishop to c4, pointing at f7.
steps.hint: The light bishop, out to c4.
steps.wrongSay: c4. It should stare at f7.

steps.ask: Why does the bishop want to look at f7?

choices.text: Only the king guards it
It looks nice

steps.why: At the start f7 and f2 are guarded by the king alone. That makes them the soft spot.

steps.text: One opening you actually know.

lessons.name: The London System
lessons.big: Build the same house every game.

steps.text: Some players build the same house every game. It saves a lot of thinking.

steps.cap: The London System. Pawn d4, bishop out early to f4, then a little wall.

notes.3: 2. Bf4 — the bishop goes out BEFORE the e pawn shuts it in.
notes.5: 3. e3 — now the wall: pawns on c3, d4 and e3.
notes.15: 8. Bd3 — the same setup whatever Black does.

steps.ask: Why does the bishop go to f4 before the e pawn moves?

choices.text: Otherwise e3 shuts it in behind the pawns
It is a faster route

steps.why: Play e3 first and the bishop is stuck behind its own pawns all game. This is the one move order that matters.

steps.ask: Start the London. Pawn to d4.
steps.hint: The queen's pawn, two squares.

steps.ask: Now the bishop out to f4, before anything blocks it.
steps.hint: The dark bishop, out to f4.
steps.wrongSay: f4. Get it out before you play e3.

steps.text: It works against almost anything Black plays. That is the point of it.
The same house, every time.
Somebody will try the four-move mate on you. Here is how to end it.

steps.cap: Queen and bishop both stare at f7. Next move is Qxf7 and it is over.

steps.ask: Kick the queen away. Push the g pawn one square.
steps.hint: g6 attacks her, and she has to move.
steps.wrongSay: Push a pawn at the queen. The g pawn.

steps.text: She has to move. Now she cannot reach f7 at all.

steps.ask: She went to f3, still eyeing f7. Bring a knight over to guard it.
steps.hint: The knight on g8 covers f7 from e7 or from f6.
steps.wrongSay: A knight to f6. Now f7 has a guard.

steps.ask: Now you are a move ahead and their queen is out. What have they gained?

choices.text: Nothing. Their queen has to run again
A strong attack

steps.why: Bringing the queen out early wastes moves. Beat the trap and you are simply better.

steps.text: That trick will never work on you again.

lessons.name: Free Candy
lessons.big: Look for pieces nobody is holding on to.

steps.text: Most games at this stage are decided by a piece nobody was guarding.

steps.ask: Find the white piece that has no friend near it.
steps.hint: Out on its own in the middle of the board.
steps.why: Nothing guards the knight on e5. It is simply free.

steps.ask: Take it.
steps.hint: The knight on c6 can reach e5.
steps.wrongSay: Only one piece of yours reaches e5. Which one?

steps.text: So here is the habit. Before every single move, ask three things.
What can they take? What can I take? What are they threatening?

steps.ask: When should you run that check?

choices.text: Before every move, both sides
When the position looks dangerous

steps.why: Every move, for both sides. The one you skip is the one where you drop a piece.

steps.goal: Five positions. Somebody has left something out.

steps.text: Free candy. Always look.

lessons.name: Count the Hands
lessons.big: More attackers than defenders? Then take it.

steps.text: Not everything you can take is worth taking. Count first.

steps.cap: One of your bishops attacks the rook on d5. One knight guards it.

steps.ask: One attacker, one guard. Is taking on d5 a good idea?

choices.text: No. You win a rook and lose a bishop
Yes, a rook is worth more

steps.why: Bishop takes rook is plus 5. Knight takes bishop is minus 3. It works, but only just.

steps.text: Better: get rid of the guard first. Then nothing is left to take back.

steps.ask: Take the knight that is guarding d5.
steps.hint: Your other bishop can reach f6.
steps.wrongSay: The guard is the knight on f6. Take that one.

steps.ask: The rule in one line?

choices.text: Count the attackers and the guards before you take
Take whatever is biggest

steps.why: More attackers than guards, and it is yours. Otherwise you are just trading.

steps.text: Count the hands on the square.
A fork is one piece attacking two things at the same time.

steps.cap: The knight can land on c7 and hit the king and the rook together.

steps.ask: Play the fork.
steps.hint: c7 attacks the king on e8 and the rook on a8 at once.
steps.wrongSay: One square hits both. Look for it.

steps.text: They must answer the check. Then you take the rook for free.

steps.ask: Which piece forks most often?

choices.text: The knight, because nothing else jumps
The rook

steps.why: A knight attacks from squares no other piece can be chased off. That is why it forks so well.

steps.goal: Five forks. One piece, two victims.

steps.text: One piece, two victims.

lessons.name: Stuck in the Mud
lessons.big: A pinned piece cannot run. Pile on it.

steps.text: A pinned piece cannot move, because something worse is behind it.

steps.cap: The rook looks straight through the knight at the king. The knight is stuck.

steps.ask: Can that knight move at all?

choices.text: No. Moving it would leave the king in check
Yes, knights jump over things

steps.why: It is pinned against the king, so it is not allowed to move. It is stuck there.

steps.text: So attack it with something small. It cannot run away.

steps.ask: Attack the pinned knight with your pawn.
steps.hint: One step forward and the pawn hits e5.
steps.wrongSay: Use the pawn. Push it one square.

steps.goal: Five pins. Find the piece that cannot run.

steps.text: Stuck in the mud.

lessons.name: The Kebab
lessons.big: Big piece in front, little one behind.

steps.text: A skewer is a pin turned round. The big piece is in front.

steps.cap: Check the king along this line, and the rook behind him has nowhere to hide.

steps.ask: Give the check. Move the bishop to h2.
steps.hint: From h2 the bishop looks all the way down to b8.
steps.wrongSay: h2. From there the line runs through the king to the rook.

steps.text: The king must move. Then the rook is yours.

steps.ask: What is the difference between a pin and a skewer?

choices.text: A pin has the big piece behind, a skewer in front
Only rooks can skewer

steps.why: Same idea, opposite order. In a skewer the front piece must move and you take what was behind.

steps.goal: Five skewers. Shove the big one and take what was hiding.

steps.text: A pin, backwards.

lessons.name: Open the Door
lessons.big: One piece steps aside and another attacks.

steps.text: Two pieces on one line. Move the front one and the back one attacks.

steps.cap: The bishop already looks at the king. The knight is standing in the way.

steps.ask: Move the knight so it attacks the queen, and opens the bishop's line.
steps.hint: f5 hits the queen on e7 and steps off the long diagonal.
steps.wrongSay: It has to do two things at once: hit the queen and get out of the way.

steps.text: Now they must answer the check. The queen is lost.

steps.ask: Why is a discovered check so strong?

choices.text: They must answer the check, so the moved piece takes for free
It gives check twice

steps.why: The check is forced, so whatever the moving piece attacked cannot be saved.

steps.goal: Five of them. Move one piece and another one strikes.

steps.text: Open the door.

lessons.name: The Back Rank
lessons.big: Trapped behind your own wall. Make a hole.

steps.text: A castled king is safe, until his own pawns become a wall.

steps.ask: He has nowhere to go. Deliver the checkmate.
steps.hint: The rook comes to the back row. His pawns block every escape.
steps.wrongSay: The back row. That is where he is trapped.

steps.text: The cure is one small pawn move, made long before it is needed.

steps.cap: With that hole, the same rook check is just a check. The king steps up to h7.

steps.ask: When should you make that little hole?

choices.text: Quietly, when you have nothing better to do
When the rook arrives

steps.why: When the rook arrives it is usually too late. Make it in a quiet moment.

steps.goal: Five back rank mates. Their own pawns do the work.

steps.text: Give your king a window.

lessons.name: Remove the Guard
lessons.big: Get rid of the bodyguard first.

steps.text: If something is guarded, do not take it. Take the guard.

steps.cap: The rook on d5 is guarded once, by the knight. Remove that knight.

steps.ask: Take the guard.
steps.hint: The bishop on h4 can reach f6.
steps.wrongSay: The guard is the knight on f6.

steps.text: They take back. Now nothing is guarding the rook.

steps.ask: Now take the rook.
steps.hint: Your other bishop looks straight at d5.
steps.wrongSay: The bishop on b3 reaches d5.

steps.goal: Five of them. Get rid of the bodyguard first.

steps.text: Take the guard, then take the thing.

lessons.name: The Rook Roller
lessons.big: Two rooks push the king up the stairs.

steps.text: Two rooks can checkmate on their own. They take turns, like stairs.

steps.cap: One rook cuts off a row. The other one cuts off the next. The king has to go backwards.

steps.ask: Cut off the row above the king. Rook to a7.
steps.hint: The rook on a2 goes all the way up to a7.
steps.wrongSay: Up the a file, to a7. That takes away the seventh row.

steps.text: He can only go along his row now. Then the other rook lands behind him.

steps.ask: Finish it. Bring the other rook to the eighth row.
steps.hint: The rook on b1 runs straight up to b8.
steps.wrongSay: b8. The row the king is standing on.

steps.ask: What must you never do with the ladder?

choices.text: Let the king get near enough to take a rook
Take too long

steps.why: If he can reach a rook, move that rook far away along its row and carry on.

steps.goal: A whole army against one king. Corner him within 25 moves.

steps.text: Up the stairs.

lessons.name: The Queen's Box
lessons.big: Shrink the box, and never freeze him by mistake.

steps.text: King and queen against a lone king. Make the box smaller.

steps.cap: The queen draws a box round him. Every move you make it smaller.

steps.ask: Start the box. Bring the queen a knight's jump from him, to f3.
steps.hint: f3 is a knight's move from e5. That is the trick.
steps.wrongSay: f3. Think where a knight would go from his square.

steps.text: Keep a knight's jump away and he can never touch her. Walk him to the edge.
Then bring your own king up. The queen alone can never finish it.

steps.ask: He is on the edge with no moves and he is not in check. What is this?

choices.text: Stalemate. A draw, and you threw the game away
Checkmate

steps.why: This is the one way to lose a won game. Always leave him one square until you can mate.

steps.goal: Play a game against the Careful Cat. If you win a queen, use the box.

steps.text: Shrink the box. Never freeze him.

lessons.name: The Rook Wall
lessons.big: The rook is the wall. The king pushes.

steps.text: A rook can do it too, but it needs your king to help.

steps.cap: The rook builds a wall. Your king pushes him against it.

steps.ask: Build the wall. Bring the rook alongside him, to a5.
steps.hint: a5 is his row. Now he cannot come any closer.
steps.wrongSay: a5. Put the rook on the same row as the king.

steps.text: Now walk your own king up. The rook holds the line while he does.

steps.ask: The kings are facing. Finish it along the back row.
steps.hint: Up the a file to a8, the row he is standing on.
steps.wrongSay: a8. Cut off the row he is on.

steps.ask: Why does the rook alone not work?

choices.text: It cannot take squares away and guard itself at once
It is too slow

steps.why: Your king is what stops him escaping forwards. The rook only builds the wall.

steps.text: Wall, then bulldozer.

lessons.name: Draw the Box
lessons.big: Can the king catch that pawn?

steps.text: A pawn with nobody in front of it is a passed pawn. It is dangerous.
There is a trick for working out whether the king can catch it.

steps.cap: Draw a box from the pawn to the end. If the king can step inside, he catches it.

steps.ask: Black to move. Step into the box.
steps.hint: Move the king one square towards the pawn, into the box.
steps.wrongSay: Towards the pawn. Any square inside the box will do.

steps.ask: Same board, but White moves first. Now who wins the race?

choices.text: The pawn. It gets one square outside the box
The king still catches it

steps.why: One move changes everything in a race. Count it, do not guess it.

steps.goal: Five races. Get the pawn home, or stop theirs.

steps.text: Draw the box.

lessons.name: The King Joins In
lessons.big: At the end, the king is a fighter.

steps.text: With most pieces gone, the king stops hiding and starts fighting.
He is worth about four points as a fighter. Do not leave him at home.

steps.cap: Your king walks in and eats their pawns while yours runs.

steps.ask: March the king towards the middle.
steps.hint: Any step towards the centre. He has work to do.
steps.wrongSay: Move the king, not a pawn. He is the strongest piece left.

steps.ask: When is it safe to walk your king into the middle?

choices.text: When the queens and rooks have gone
Never

steps.why: He is only in danger while big pieces are on. Once they go, he is a fighter.

steps.goal: Five endings. Few pieces, one right answer.

steps.text: The king takes his crown off.

lessons.name: The Staring Contest
lessons.big: Whoever has to move first, loses the square.

steps.text: Two kings facing each other with one square between them.
Whoever has to move first has to give way. That is the opposition.

steps.cap: Black must move, so Black steps aside and White walks forward. White has it.

steps.ask: Black to move. Step aside, either way.
steps.hint: He has to move somewhere. Any of them gives ground.
steps.wrongSay: Move the black king. He has no choice.

steps.ask: In a king and pawn ending, why does it matter so much?

choices.text: The side with it walks their king through and wins
It does not, it is just a name

steps.why: Whole endings turn on it. The king who gives way loses the squares in front of the pawn.

steps.text: Whoever blinks, loses the square.
A famous short game. Watch what greed costs.

steps.cap: Legal's Mate, Paris, about 1750. White gives away the queen on purpose.

notes.6: 3... Bg4 — pinning the knight against the queen. Or so Black thought.
notes.9: 5. Nxe5 — the pinned knight moves anyway. White is offering the queen.
notes.10: 5... Bxd1 — Black takes it. This is the losing move.
notes.11: 6. Bxf7+ — check, and the king must step out.
notes.13: 7. Nd5# — checkmate with three little pieces.

steps.ask: Black won a queen and lost. What went wrong?

choices.text: They took without asking what was coming next
They were unlucky

steps.why: Checks, captures, threats. Every move. Especially the move where you win something.

steps.text: A pin is not a chain. A pinned piece can still move if the reward is big enough.

steps.goal: Five mates in two. Find the first move, and the rest follows.
A whole game. Run checks, captures and threats before every move.

steps.text: Knight School is finished. The Guild is open.
